system:
You are a computational cancer biologist searching CRISPR screen data for selective genetic dependencies: genes that cancer cells with a particular alteration (the biomarker) need more than other cancer cells do. Such genes are candidate drug targets with a built-in patient-selection strategy.

Work like a careful scientist:
1. Plan first with write_plan, and revise it as you learn.
2. Survey the data (genome_wide_top, scan_biomarker, scan_target) to generate candidate hypotheses.
3. Be sceptical before you believe a signal. Use inspect_association to check whether it is driven by one lineage or a disease subtype hiding inside a lineage, and whether the effect is large enough to matter. Ask whether the biology makes sense (paralog buffering, pathway dependence, oncogene addiction). A broadly essential target may lack a therapeutic window.
4. Check the literature with search_pubmed before registering, and judge novelty honestly.
5. Register only your best hypotheses (register_hypothesis). Registration is final and must come before replication. You have 5 replications, each of which must pass one-sided p < 0.01 in BOTH held-out Broad cell lines and independent Sanger screens.
6. Report honestly with submit_findings. A hypothesis is replicated only if replicate() said so. Negative results are results. Never let what you remember from the literature override what the data show.

You have at most 15 model turns. Batch independent tool calls in one turn.
task_prompt:
Patient population of interest: cancers with biomarker HOT_BRAF (BRAF hotspot mutation).

Find the single best candidate therapeutic target for this population: the gene these cell lines depend on most selectively, supported by the data. Register your top candidate (you may register up to two), replicate it, and submit findings with your best candidate listed first.

content.thinking: I had registered the novelty as "well_established," but that's inaccurate; the literature is only partially known, since a DUSP4/DUSP6 paralog dependency paper exists and BRAF-specific DUSP4 dependency is partly covered. I can't re-register, so I'll state novelty as partially_known in the submission and note the discrepancy there. Now I'll run the replication.

The Sanger effect is weaker here, with a beta of -0.12 and p=0.005, but it still clears the 0.01 threshold, so the result replicates with a smaller effect in that dataset. BRAF shows up as the strongest selective dependency, though it is already the known oncogene and the canonical target of BRAF inhibitors, so it isn't a new finding. I'll submit with a confidence of about 0.6 and report that the Sanger effect is weaker.

findings.claim: BRAF hotspot-mutant lines depend on DUSP4 (lineage-adjusted t=-8.8 in discovery; mean effect -0.81 altered vs -0.02 other). Replicated in held-out Broad lines (beta -0.50, p=5e-11) and in Sanger (beta -0.12, p=0.005, a much weaker effect that passes the p<0.01 threshold only narrowly). Plausible mechanism: DUSP4 is an ERK-induced brake on MAPK output, and a paralog-buffered DUSP4/DUSP6 dependency has been reported (PMID 34857952; DUSP4 protecting BRAF/NRAS melanoma, PMID 35580987).

input.summary: Best candidate for HOT_BRAF cancers: DUSP4. The strongest dependency overall is BRAF itself (beta -0.95, 86% of altered lines dependent), but that is the driver oncogene and is already the established therapeutic target, so it was not counted as a new candidate. Among non-self genes, DUSP4 was the most selective: altered lines are strongly dependent (mean -0.81 vs -0.02 in others), with the signal concentrated in melanoma (27 of 50 altered lines are skin). DUSP4 replicated in held-out Broad lines with a strong effect. In the independent Sanger screen the effect was much weaker, so confidence is moderate. Novelty is partially known, since DUSP4/DUSP6 digenic dependence in MAPK-driven cancers is already published. Note: the registration call was recorded as 'well_established' because of a tool-argument issue on my side; my assessment is partially_known. MAP2K1, MAPK1 and PEA15 also showed MAPK-pathway dependencies (MAPK1 replicated-level signal not tested). Only one hypothesis was registered and replicated.
